summary: IEEE 802.1Qca Path Control and Reservation provides explicit path control in Layer 2 networks, going beyond shortest paths from 802.1aq. This standards-track RFC defines how IS-IS carries the information to set up and control explicit forwarding trees.

eli5.summary: Usually traffic takes the shortest road. This lets someone choose a specific route and reserve it, with IS-IS telling the switches.

questions: what is is-is path control and reservation
what is an explicit tree in layer 2
what sub-tlvs does is-is pcr define
subtitle: The IS-IS sub-TLVs that let a path computation element dictate explicit forwarding trees in Layer 2 networks.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.1aq Shortest Path Bridging only forwards along shortest paths, so operators cannot steer traffic along chosen paths or record bandwidth for them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7813 defines five IS-IS sub-TLVs (Topology, Hop, Bandwidth Constraint, Bandwidth Assignment, Timestamp) that carry an explicit tree description in a Link State PDU, flooded like other SPB information.
tldr.outcome: Bridges install forwarding entries for strict or loose explicit trees, or for Maximally Redundant Trees, as specified by IEEE 802.1Qca. The RFC adds no security beyond what IS-IS already has.

today: RFC 7813 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It defines the IS-IS encoding for the behaviour specified in IEEE 802.1Qca.

sections.title: IS-IS PCR in Context
sections.content:
IEEE 802.1Qca Path Control and Reservation (PCR) extends IS-IS to control Explicit Trees (ETs) in Layer 2 networks. It is compatible with Shortest Path Bridging (SPB) as specified in RFC 6329 and IEEE 802.1aq, and relies on the SPB architecture, terminology and some of its sub-TLVs. PCR only addresses point-to-point physical links.

This RFC specifies the five new sub-TLVs. PCR also reuses SPB sub-TLVs for link metrics and for the associations among bridges, MAC addresses, VLAN IDs (VIDs) and I-SIDs. A bridge does not need the full IS-IS SPB protocol, only those sub-TLVs, and can support SPB and PCR at once in the same IS-IS entity, per instance. The RFC says IS-IS PCR has no impact on IETF protocols.
sections.eli5: Switches already talk to each other with a protocol called IS-IS. This document adds new kinds of notes to that conversation so a planner can choose routes.

sections.title: Explicit Trees and the PCE
sections.content:
An Explicit Tree is an undirected, loop-free topology whose use is controlled by associating VIDs and MAC addresses with it. It MUST NOT contain cycles. Trees are typically determined by a Path Computation Element (PCE), which acts through a Path Control Agent (PCA) that is part of the IS-IS domain. Each tree has exactly one owner PCE. The PCE or PCA MUST establish an IS-IS adjacency so it receives all LSPs, and sets up a tree by injecting an LSP that carries it. How the PCE computes trees, and how it talks to a PCA, is not specified.

A tree is either strict, specifying all bridges and paths, or loose, specifying only bridges with a special role (Edge Bridge, root, leaf, a bridge to avoid, or a transit hop). Bridges compute the paths of a loose tree with their Bridge Local Computation Engine, using the shortest path unless a constraint says otherwise.

Trees are refreshed like other IS-IS data because of LSP aging. A PCE withdraws a tree by sending an LSP without its Topology sub-TLV. If a tree cannot be installed, for example because a constraint cannot be met or the sub-TLV is ill-formed, no tree is installed and a management report is generated.
sections.eli5: A planner draws a route map with no loops. Some maps list every street, and some only list the stops and let each switch find its own streets between them.

sections.title: The Explicit ECT Algorithms
sections.content:
A VLAN's control mode is chosen by associating its Base VID with an ECT Algorithm in the SPB Base VLAN-Identifiers sub-TLV. An ECT Algorithm value is the IEEE 802.1 OUI 00-80-C2 followed by an index. There are five explicit ones.

  • Strict Tree (ST), 00-80-C2-17: MUST be used for a strict tree. It is static, so the owner PCE must detect topology changes and reinstall the tree.
  • Loose Tree (LT), range 00-80-C2-21 to 00-80-C2-30: MAY be supported. One loose tree, maintained by IS-IS, with the root indicated in the Topology sub-TLV.
  • Loose Tree Set (LTS), range 00-80-C2-31 to 00-80-C2-40: MAY be supported. One loose tree rooted at each Edge Bridge.
  • MRT, 00-80-C2-18: MAY be supported. Maximally Redundant Trees computed in a distributed way with the MRT Lowpoint algorithm of RFC 7811.
  • MRTG, 00-80-C2-19: MAY be supported. The GADAG is computed by a single entity and flooded, and bridges derive the MRTs from it.

LT and LTS use shortest paths after pruning links that fail the constraints, with the tie-breaking of RFC 6329, which is why they have ranges of values. If the SPB Link Metric values at the two ends of an adjacency differ, the maximum MUST be used.
sections.eli5: There are five rulebooks for building a route, from write-every-street to let-the-switches-figure-it-out. A code number on each VLAN says which rulebook it follows.

sections.title: The Topology and Hop Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
An explicit tree MUST be described by the variable-length Topology sub-TLV (type 21), carried in an MT-Capability TLV (type 144) in a Link State PDU. It holds a count of Base VIDs, each a 12-bit value preceded by 4 reserved bits, then further sub-TLVs: two or more Hop sub-TLVs and optional constraints. An ill-formed one is ignored and reported.

Each Hop sub-TLV (type 22) names a bridge by its 6-byte IS-IS System ID. A strict tree is split into branches, each a point-to-point path ending at a leaf. The first hop is the root, and a hop is created only if that bridge is directly connected to the previous one. A flags byte holds six one-bit flags: Circuit (C), VID (V), Edge Bridge (B), Root (R), Leaf (L) and Exclude (E), plus 2 reserved bits. The Circuit flag adds a 4-byte Extended Local Circuit ID to pick between parallel links in a strict tree. The VID flag adds per-VID Transmit and Receive flags for Edge Bridges that differ from the default. A Hop sub-TLV that is 6 bytes longer than normal carries a delay constraint, a Unidirectional Link Delay sub-TLV from RFC 7810, usable with a single loose tree.

For a loose tree, the root MUST be the first hop and the leaves MUST be listed. Exclude marks a bridge to avoid, and the Exclude and Root flags cannot both be set on a hop.
sections.eli5: The topology note is the whole route plan. Each hop note names one switch and says what job it has, like start, end, or stay away.

sections.title: Bandwidth and Timestamp Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Bandwidth Constraint sub-TLV (type 23, length 5) tells bridges how much available bandwidth a loose tree must provide, either in total or for one traffic class given by the PCP field. Each loose hop MUST meet it. A DEI bit chooses committed rate when clear, peak rate when set.

The Bandwidth Assignment sub-TLV (type 24, length 5) records a bandwidth assignment at each hop of the tree. It carries a PCP, a DEI bit, a 3-bit Importance field (lower is more important, default 7) and the bandwidth. Both bandwidth values are 32-bit IEEE floating-point numbers in bytes per second. If the assignment would overbook any link, it MUST NOT be performed and a management report is generated, though a valid new tree is still installed. Recording bandwidth is optional, and IS-IS and MSRP MUST NOT both make bandwidth assignments in the same domain.

When assignments conflict, precedence is ordered by PCP, then Importance, then the optional Timestamp sub-TLV (type 25, length 4), a 4-byte count of seconds since the PTP epoch of 1970-01-01 00:00:00 TAI. An assignment with a higher PCP, higher Importance or earlier timestamp wins. If that cannot resolve it, the PCE whose LSP has the numerically lowest LSP ID wins.
sections.eli5: You can also say how wide the road must be and reserve space on it. If two planners want the same space, rules decide who goes first, and the earlier request wins a tie.

sections.title: Distributing a GADAG for MRT-FRR
sections.content:
The same sub-TLVs can carry the data for Fast Reroute with Maximally Redundant Trees. The MRT Lowpoint algorithm first computes a GADAG (Generalized Almost Directed Acyclic Graph), then two trees, MRT-Blue and MRT-Red, per MRT root. The GADAG is identical for all trees in a domain, so with the MRTG algorithm a single GADAG Computer, either a PCE or the GADAG Root, MUST compute it and flood a Topology sub-TLV describing it.

The bridge with the numerically lowest BridgeID MUST be the GADAG Root, and the Bridge Priority part of the ID lets operators choose it. The GADAG is encoded by directed ear decomposition: the first hop is the GADAG Root, the first ear starts and ends at the root, and each later ear ends at nodes from earlier ears. A GADAG has no leaves, so the Leaf flag marks the end of a block instead. Block IDs are rebuilt while parsing, starting at 0 for the root.

IS-IS PCR does not use the MRT Profile of RFC 7812. It relies only on the algorithm in RFC 7811. Equal-cost ties are broken by the lower BridgeID, an 8-byte value made of a 2-byte priority and the 6-byte System ID.
sections.eli5: For a backup plan, one switch draws a map with two routes to every place, then tells everyone. Each switch uses that map to work out its own backup roads.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it adds no security risks to IS-IS and provides no extra security for IS-IS in a configured environment or single-operator domain such as a data center. IS-IS PCR is not for zero-configuration environments.

Any mechanism that chooses forwarding paths and allocates resources is potentially vulnerable to attack. The PCE security considerations in RFC 4655 should be consulted. Because tree information travels in IS-IS, the IS-IS security considerations of RFC 1195 and mechanisms such as RFC 5310 for authenticating peer advertisements apply.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can steer traffic could cause trouble, so the same locks that protect IS-IS need to protect these messages too.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The five sub-TLVs are defined inside the MT-Capability TLV (type 144) and listed in the IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry. The Topology and Hop sub-TLVs have variable length. The Bandwidth Constraint and Bandwidth Assignment sub-TLVs have length 5, and the Timestamp sub-TLV has length 4.
sections.eli5: Each new kind of note gets its own official number so every switch recognizes it.

items.label: Topology
items.desc: Describes an explicit tree; variable length.

items.desc: Names one bridge and its role; variable length.

items.label: Bandwidth Constraint
items.desc: Available bandwidth a loose tree must provide; length 5.

items.label: Bandwidth Assignment
items.desc: Bandwidth to record at each hop; length 5.

items.label: Timestamp
items.desc: Seconds since the PTP epoch; length 4.

items.label: ST
items.desc: Strict Tree; a single strict explicit tree.

items.label: MRT

items.label: MRTG
items.desc: MRTs derived from a flooded GADAG.

items.label: LT
items.desc: Loose Tree; one loose explicit tree.

items.label: LTS
items.desc: Loose Tree Set; a loose tree rooted at each Edge Bridge.
